clinicalPearls: The most common form of nontuberculous mycobacterial disease in many regions, caused predominantly by Mycobacterium avium complex, followed by M. kansasii, M. xenopi, M. malmoense, and M. abscessus
Two classic radiological phenotypes are recognised: fibrocavitary upper-lobe disease and nodular-bronchiectatic disease
Fibrocavitary disease typically affects older male smokers with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and resembles tuberculosis
Nodular-bronchiectatic disease classically affects older non-smoking women, often tall and slender, with right-middle-lobe and lingular involvement (so-called Lady Windermere syndrome)
Hot-tub lung is a hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled mycobacteria in aerosolised water and is distinct from invasive infection
Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms, characteristic imaging, exclusion of other causes, and defined microbiological criteria, since a single positive culture may reflect colonisation
Treatment is prolonged macrolide-based multidrug therapy, continued for about a year beyond culture conversion, with the regimen tailored to the species
Not every isolate needs treatment; the decision weighs disease severity, progression, species, and the risks of long, poorly tolerated therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease arises when ubiquitous environmental mycobacteria from water and soil are inhaled and establish infection in a susceptible airway. The main predisposing factor is impaired local defence from structural lung disease such as bronchiectasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cystic fibrosis, or prior tuberculosis, rather than systemic immunodeficiency. The organisms provoke a granulomatous inflammatory response that produces either upper-lobe cavitation resembling tuberculosis or a nodular-bronchiectatic pattern with tree-in-bud change, particularly in the right middle lobe and lingula. Because exposure is universal but disease is focal and typically non-disseminating, host airway factors and body habitus are thought to be central; a separate hypersensitivity response to aerosolised organisms underlies hot-tub lung.
additionalDifferentials: Other chronic pulmonary infection such as nocardiosis
additionalInvestigations: Repeated sputum mycobacterial cultures (at least two separate positive samples) to meet diagnostic criteria
Bronchoalveolar lavage culture when sputum is unobtainable or non-diagnostic
High-resolution CT of the chest for cavitation, nodules, and bronchiectasis
Molecular identification to species (and, for M. abscessus, subspecies) level
Species-specific susceptibility testing, notably macrolide for MAC and rifampicin for M. kansasii
Lung biopsy with granulomatous inflammation plus culture when criteria are otherwise unmet
Assessment of underlying lung disease and, in atypical cases, immune status
redFlags: Extensive cavitary disease with haemoptysis and weight loss
Infection with a drug-resistant species such as M. abscessus with inducible macrolide resistance
Disease in cystic fibrosis affecting transplantation candidacy
Deterioration or macrolide resistance during treatment indicating inadequate therapy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by species and phenotype: M. kansasii responds well to rifampicin-based therapy, nodular-bronchiectatic MAC is often controllable though relapse and reinfection are common, and fibrocavitary or M. abscessus disease carries a worse outlook with lower cure rates. Underlying lung disease and treatment tolerance strongly influence long-term outcomes.
pitfalls: Treating a single positive culture without meeting diagnostic criteria, mistaking colonisation for disease
Using macrolide-containing regimens without recognising or testing for inducible macrolide resistance in rapid growers
Adding a single new drug to a failing regimen and thereby selecting resistance
Failing to identify the species and subspecies, which determines the regimen and expected response
Underestimating the toxicity and duration of therapy and losing adherence
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
British Thoracic Society guideline for the management of nontuberculous mycobacterial pulmonary disease
management: Treat Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease with a macrolide plus rifampicin and ethambutol, continued well beyond sputum culture conversion
Add intravenous or nebulised amikacin for cavitary, extensive or refractory MAC disease
Use rifampicin-based multidrug therapy for M. kansasii and macrolide plus intravenous agents such as amikacin, cefoxitin or imipenem for M. abscessus
Manage hot-tub lung by removing the aerosolised-water exposure, using corticosteroids rather than prolonged antimycobacterials
Optimise the underlying lung disease with airway clearance and physiotherapy for bronchiectasis and appropriate bronchodilator therapy
Consider watchful waiting for mild nodular-bronchiectatic disease and surgical resection for localised refractory or cavitary disease
Monitor serial sputum cultures for conversion and screen for drug toxicity, managing through a specialist multidisciplinary team

Red flag present (haemoptysis, weight loss, rapid progression, resistant species)?
Urgent review for haemoptysis; exclude tuberculosis
Repeated sputum cultures, bronchoscopic lavage if needed, species identification
Two or more positive cultures with compatible imaging?
Consider colonisation, tuberculosis or aspergillosis; re-culture
Macrolide, rifampicin and ethambutol for MAC disease
Intravenous agents for extensive or severe disease
Varies by species; kansasii responds well, MAC is often controllable but relapses
